questions.stem: (1) In the transcriptions, pear and “this pear” show [pʰ], while spare and despair show [p⁼]; explain these diacritics and infer the aspiration rule. (2) Compare “a redcoat”/“a red coat” and “a bluebird”/“a blue bird.” (3) Describe particle movement using “John turned off the machine” and “John turned the machine off”; say whether event meaning changes. (4) Explain: Diner: “Waiter, what's this fly doing in my soup?” Waiter: “Madam, I believe that's the backstroke.”
questions.referenceAnswer: Raised h marks aspiration and raised = marks unaspirated sounds; voiceless stops are aspirated at the start of a stressed syllable. Compounds take primary stress on the first part and may have lexicalized meaning (redcoat = British soldier), unlike literal adjective+noun phrases. Particle movement places the particle after the object without changing core event meaning. The waiter answers the literal reading of an indirect complaint, creating the joke; the source calls it a quantity-maxim flout.
